I'm in Santiago, Chile at 2026-03-16 07:30 -03 (UTC-0300) (2026-03-16T10:30:00Z in UTC), at latitude -33.4489 degrees and longitude -70.6693 degrees. It says the Moon's altitude is 28.227 degrees and its azimuth is 89.613 degrees, so it is above the horizon. The Moon is 8.04 percent illuminated, 32.867 degrees from the Sun, and 382363 kilometers away. Based on the data you provided, **yes, you should be able to see the Moon quite clearly.**

Here is the breakdown of why it will be visible to you:

### 1. Position in the Sky
The Moon is at an **altitude of 28.2 degrees**. In practical terms, this means it is well above the horizon (about 1/3 of the way up toward the zenith). It is not "hugging" the horizon where atmospheric haze or buildings would obstruct it.

### 2. Direction
The **azimuth is 89.6 degrees**, which is almost exactly **Due East**. Since the Sun is still below the horizon (at -2.8 degrees), the eastern sky will be the brightest part of the horizon, but the Moon will be high enough to stand out against the sky.

### 3. Visibility vs. Brightness
You mentioned the Moon is only **8.04% illuminated**. While this is a very thin crescent, it is still a celestial object reflecting sunlight. Because it is in **Civil Twilight**, the sky is still relatively bright (the sun is only about 3 degrees below the horizon). 
*   **The Challenge:** In civil twilight, the sky has a lot of "ambient" light. A very thin crescent can sometimes be harder to see than a half-moon because it doesn't have as much surface area to reflect light.
*   **The Advantage:** Because the Moon is 28 degrees up, it is far enough away from the "glow" of the horizon to be distinct.

### 4. Local Conditions
Since you noted the **sky is clear** and you are an **ordinary adult with normal eyesight**, there are no significant physical barriers to seeing it.

### Summary Verdict:
**You should be able to see it.** Look toward the **East**. Because it is a thin crescent (8%) and it is still relatively bright outside (Civil Twilight), it might not "pop" as intensely as it would in total darkness, but it should be clearly visible as a silver sliver in the eastern sky.
